source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; incidental details generalised; question in yes/no form.

suggested_action: buy a kidney on the black market
kept: You are the patient, after years of dialysis; no family match exists and a minor heart attack makes an official transplant virtually impossible.
People from poor countries sell to wealthy buyers through an organised but illegal market that exploits poverty.
Medical risks are low; donors can live with one kidney but have restrictions and more fragile health.
Without buying you die in a few years; with buying both you and donor probably live well for decades.
You personally gain survival by purchasing; clinicians perform removal, and the donor bears health costs rather than being the recipient.
The suggested action is to buy a black-market kidney.
rewrite: You have been dependent on dialysis for the past several years because your kidneys have failed. You cannot receive a kidney from anyone in your family because none of them is a suitable organ donor. Many patients die on the official waiting list before receiving one. A minor heart attack has moved you still farther down that list, making a transplant through it virtually impossible. You consider the black market, where poor people in poorer countries sell kidneys to wealthy buyers. Medical risks are low. A donor can live with one kidney but will face medical limitations and more fragile health. This well-organised market is illegal because it pressures people in poverty to endanger their health. If you do not buy a kidney, you will die in a few years. If you buy one, you and the donor will probably both live well for decades. You would, however, be exploiting the donor’s poverty. Do you buy a kidney from the black market?

generalised.why: chronic dependence remains without an exact duration

notes: Deliberately retained: kidney failure, dialysis, the minor heart attack’s effect on eligibility, one kidney left to the donor, low medical risk and probably decades of life for both; these set the medical alternatives, survival benefit and donor harm.
